utterances.text: Have you heard of a unit called the Mountain Battalion of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers who were protecting you, who were with your group, were they members of that Mountain Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no other questions to ask of this witness. Thank you, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Will there be any redirect, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There will be none, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I understood you said that your father did not survive.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that many people did not survive, thousands or whatever. How do you know they did not survive? Do you have any news? Or perhaps they are somewhere.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't think that they have survived. They have been missing for five years, and I think that they were executed like everybody else, that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, speaking of execution, you mentioned that the soldiers would take the Muslim prisoners behind the tank and they would come back without them. But did you hear shots, or were they slaughtered by knife? How did you understand the situation?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: No shooting could be heard, so I think they did it with a knife or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But no evidence was there. You did not see blood around; you didn't hear shouts, cries. When people are slaughtered, they can react. Did you feel anything? What was the atmosphere like? Of course, they did not disappear by enchantment, but how was it? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: It happened in a simple way. They would come and take men away and the person would never come back. And we didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were all in the same --

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: They would come -- yes, on the meadow, near the tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: On the meadow, near the tank. If they were killed, how could they hide them? Where did they hide them?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you anything about that. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it in the woods that they could hide them, or you could see the corpses? Was it an open air place where you could see people or a place in the woods so that nobody could see the other?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: It was a cornfield, maize field, not a forest, where they took people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the maize was high, it could hide a person.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Then, concerning your father, you are sure he did not survive? Did they find his corpse, or did some people inform you that he did not survive? Can we still hope that he is alive?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: I can always hope, but judging by the kind of people who were there, I very much doubt that he would have survived. I didn't hear anything and he has not been identified as one of the killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned something rather important. You said that some of the soldiers were in the Serbian military uniform. Do you mean the military uniform of the Serbian army or of the Bosnian Serb army? Because there is a difference. Do you know the difference?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were members of the Serb army, that is, the army of the Bosnian Serbs. But I couldn't tell you the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you see any badge on them to indicate which division they were from? Or this was something too difficult at that time.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: It was difficult. I could only see some kind of black ribbons on their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they were, I think, as you said, in camouflage, black and green; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was this indicative of a certain group of military people, of a certain division which you knew about?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it was indicative of one particular group because there was a group of people who were wearing the same uniforms and those black ribbons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the group?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in one of the exhibits which we saw, the pictures or the movie, there was a very interesting answer of a soldier to another soldier, when one of them was saying, "3.000 have surrendered and the people in Belgrade think we exaggerate." Now, what is the people of Belgrade's business with Srebrenica? Do you have an idea?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think they had direct influence on all that, that they were allies of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the soldiers were speaking about Belgrade as if they come from there or what?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: In a different sense, I think, that they -- that they were informed about the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, the last question: When you said that the soldiers were taking people behind the tank and they disappeared after that, whom did -- was there any kind of preference or priorities? Whom did they take? Would they take -- did they choose just something like guessing or taking people, a certain kind of people? For instance, people who prove to be military or that sort of thing or young. Was there any indication whom they were looking for?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: They took people at random as they pleased. I know that this young man in a T-shirt was taken away probably because they thought he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they took other people who were not soldiers, who could not be soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They couldn't be soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean old or children or boys or what?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Also elderly people and young people. People who were dressed in civilian clothes who were not soldiers and whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Husic. Thank you. I hope your father will come back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, when you started out from Srebrenica with the -- or near Srebrenica with the column of men that were going to go through the woods, did you know the reason why it had been decided that the men who would go through the woods on their own to try to reach Tuzla, and the women and children would be helped to get along to the UN Compound in Potocari? I mean what -- did anybody say out loud what was the basis for that decision since everybody, obviously, wanted to get out and get into the free territory? Do you know why it was decided to have a column of men go through the woods and have the women and children go ahead and the elderly go ahead to the UN Compound?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know why a decision like that had been reached. I simply followed those men together with my brother and my father. And the main objective of our breakthrough through the woods was to save ourselves because it was believed that the women and children would not be harmed in Potocari. And we knew that they would be transported to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But there was, I gather, from your answer, a fear that if the men went with the women and the children up to Potocari, that harm would befall them as opposed to the women and children; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When Judge Riad asked you about how you knew that many of the people you talked about or identified did not survive, could you tell us approximately or about how many people you saw the soldiers pull out of the crowd or the column, take away behind the cornfields or in the cornfields behind the tank, you saw something actually done to them to the extent they were taken away, as opposed to people that you just have no idea what happened to them, they just disappeared?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: You mean from the meadow, concerning the people who were taken away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to them after I left the meadow. I don't know what was their fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My question would be how many people did you actually see Serb soldiers take out of the meadow or take out of the column that was going along, take them away and then you never saw them again?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Several of them would take them away. One of the men was taken away by two people, two men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you one final question about that. Would you say that you saw that happen, you saw a Muslim man taken either out of the meadow or away from the column by soldiers, singled out and taken away? Would you say six, twelve, I don't know, how many, about?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: No, I saw between four and six of such cases that I saw personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the rest of the people that you say did not survive, it means that they were either in the meadow or in the column and then they were just never seen again, that you know about. Right?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Husic, I have two questions for you. While you were still in the woods, at one point in time you heard soldiers speaking about a surrender, that you should surrender because the UNPROFOR soldiers would protect you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So before you surrendered, did you have an opportunity to see the soldiers or at least the individuals whom you believed to be UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were walking up and down the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could you then tell us what tilted the balance in favour of the decision to surrender, because you were insisting -- the fact that you saw them, did you insist because of that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, if we hadn't seen the UN soldiers and the UN personnel carrier, we probably wouldn't surrender. But there was some hope because of the presence of UNPROFOR, and we thought that they would not dare kill us all in their presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was your reaction when you finally realised that they were not UNPROFOR soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew what was in store for us. I realised that we had been lured down to the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. My second question is the following: A soldier told you at one point that Alija was not there to protect you but that you will wait and that you will see Ratko Mladic, who would arrive to the meadow. What was your reaction to those words? Did you believe that Ratko Mladic would come or not?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: We believed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why? Why did you believe that?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Because whatever they said, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when were the threats made?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: At the moment we came down to the meadow, a Serb soldier at one point said, "Wait until General Mladic comes here."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember what language the soldiers spoke?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: You mean -- yeah, they were speaking Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was there a distant accent by which you could tell where they were from?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Witness. I don't have any other questions. We are aware of the fact that you have lived through some terrible events. You have answered questions that were put to you by the Prosecutor, by the Defence, and by the Judges. Is there anything else, Witness, that you wish to say? Is there anything that have you not had opportunity to say so far?

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: I believe I have said everything that I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, very much. I believe that there are some exhibits to be taken care of. Witness, could you please stay here a while. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are a number of exhibits. There are three film clips which are Prosecutor's Exhibit 101, 102, and 103 and companion transcripts, 101, 102, and 103A. Then there is Prosecutor's Exhibit 104 which is a still photograph taken from the Prosecutor's Exhibit 103 showing the witness, himself. There is Prosecutor's Exhibits 105, 106, and 107, a series of still images showing Bosnian Serb soldiers in stolen Dutch UN flak jackets. Prosecutor's Exhibits 108, 109, 110, 111, pictures of people who surrendered alive to the Bosnian Serb army and who have not been heard of since, and who are known to this witness by name. We would move into evidence each of those exhibits, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Mr. Dubuisson, the exhibits mentioned by the Prosecutor, will be admitted into evidence. Will you please take note of that. Thank you. Mr. Husic, you're still a very young man and you will probably live a very long life. We would like to congratulate you that you have survived, and I know -- hope that you are aware of the importance of the role that you have to tell the story that you have been through. All these events should be condemned. They cannot be tolerated by humanity. We would just like to thank you once again for coming here to testify and wish you a safe journey home. The usher will show you out of the courtroom. Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: ENVER HUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that -- I hope you have another witness, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, we have another witness, Mr. President, a protected witness. Mr. McCloskey will lead the evidence with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have worked for 40 minutes. Perhaps we should begin with that testimony and then after that, we will have a longer break so as to manage the time available to us in the best possible manner. Can we have the witness brought in, please? I should like us first to specify the protective measures that are requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness will require a pseudonym and face distortion, so the courtroom will have to be prepared for the witness to arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are aware of the proposal of the prosecution and we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, it would perhaps be better to have a 20-minute break and when we resume, the Judges will already have the witness in the courtroom. So a 20-minute break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness L. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. The registrar is going to show you a piece of paper with your name written on it. Please tell us only whether that is your name by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, that is, indeed, your name. Is that your name, Witness L?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you will be answering questions put to you by Mr. McCloskey, the Prosecutor, who is standing to your right. Mr. McCloskey, I give you the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I get to the witness, one small piece of business from yesterday. We apparently discovered some French translations of yesterday's protective witness' medical records, which I offer as evidence under seal, Exhibit 118A and 117B, which I believe have been provided to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dubuisson, do you have the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I'm going to distribute them to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Are you in a position to start, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Mr. President, is there a particular time you think you might want to break so that I can try to anticipate that, or do you want to just see how it goes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A very good question, and thank you. Perhaps halfway along we'll have a 15-minute break. We've already, I think, have three breaks today, so we'll have a fourth. Today is going to be an exception. We'll make a break about halfway along of about 15 minutes, so you can control your time. Thank you. Examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness L, none of that involved you, but it's now time to ask you some questions, to have your testimony. First of all, can you tell us where you're from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I'm from the municipality of Zvornik, the village of [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your birth date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was born on the [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the war breaking out, you were living in the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was working in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Ratko Mitrovic ^.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you worked for that company prior to the breaking out of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I worked there for 18 years and several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of work was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was a construction worker. I was a skilled worker for reinforced concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war started, when did you move to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I moved to Srebrenica on the 14th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living on July 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, 1995, I was living in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I was living with two brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation? How did you keep yourself alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We lived off the land, we farmed the land, and we also received some humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the three brothers in your family in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, one of my brothers, but he was a cook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the three brothers decide to do on July 11th when the town was falling to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: One of my brothers was disabled. He was not disabled during the war; he had a bad leg. He went to Potocari, surrendered to UNPROFOR. And the other brother headed, together with me, into the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your brothers make it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. This one who was disabled, he was allowed to cross into our territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about your other brother, the brother that was a cook in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The other brother was with me. He was captured together with me, and I don't know anything as to what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you decide to do on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: On July the 11th, when Srebrenica fell, we decided to travel towards the free territory of Tuzla, through the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did you first go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We first went to a rally in the village of Susnjari, municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the decision-making process that the men took to decide to rally there around Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know, because the commanders must have known. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Susnjari, about what time did you get there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We got there in the evening, perhaps it was around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that evening of July 11th, when you got to this area --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- are you able to give any kind of an estimate of how many people were gathered in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: According to an estimate, there were between 10.000 and 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an estimate someone's told you, or is that your personal estimate from actually looking at the crowd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, it was our personal estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "our", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I mean myself, I mean mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any women or children in that crowd, or was it mostly men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: There were only men, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell how many men were armed with weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: There were some with weapons but I don't know the number. Maybe 200, 300. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the ones that were within your area of vision; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there could have been many more than 200.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't even see them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any commanders make any decisions or announce anything to the group while you were there in Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: What happened was that when we arrived, that evening columns were formed, I heard from this other men, that they started leaving around midnight. My column left in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many people were in that first column or group of men that left at midnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know because the column went continuously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't leave the Susnjari area until the afternoon of the following day. That would be July 12th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. It was a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many people were in your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know because as one group left, another went after it. So it would be difficult to tell how many men were in each group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why the men decided to go through the woods the way they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Because we didn't dare go to Potocari, because we saw the situation, that they had threatened us that if Srebrenica fell, that they would settle accounts with the able-bodied men, and that is, anyway, what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you finally got started in your group, on the 12th, can you describe the journey through the woods until you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we started from Susnjari, we were going for about 300 metres and then we entered the woods called Buljim. Shortly after that the column stopped. When we stopped, men asked that the few remaining people with weapons should go in front. And those people who were going in front of me saw some dead bodies and they became afraid. Then those under arms went off and we didn't see them again. I don't know whether they abandoned us or what; we don't know. We continued for along as we could see, while the daylight lasted. And then when darkness fell, I spent the night under an oak tree, and then the next day I found a group of people, among whom was my brother. Then shortly after that, Serb soldiers started calling out over the loudspeakers for us to surrender. As we didn't have any loudspeakers, our men would tell them aloud that we would surrender if UNPROFOR or the Red Cross were there. They didn't respond. They gave us an ultimatum, a deadline, until 10.00; then they postponed it to 1500 hours. As we thought that the situation was hopeless, the men decided to surrender. As we were coming down, Serb soldiers came onto the road. They were all in uniform, camouflage uniform, and first they asked us to give them any money we had, German marks or dollars or any other foreign currency. Those who had anything gave it up; those who didn't, they didn't. Then they threatened, "If we find money on someone who didn't surrender it," they would suffer the same fate as those before them. Then women and children were passing by the road, as we were standing by the road. And then they ordered us to raise our hands up. After a while, they gave us orders to run for some 50 metres and then go uphill, where we found a large group of people sitting there. So they ordered us to sit down and form lines and rows, and once we did, a Serb soldier, with a scarf on his head -- he was somewhere between 20 and 22 -- he told me that the governments were negotiating an exchange on the principle "all for all". When all of the people had gathered there -- according to my estimate, it was about 2.000 to 2.500 people -- then this Serb soldier again told us, and on his sleeve it said "The army of Republika Srpska." When those soldiers were changing shifts --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Let me take you back and ask you a couple of clarifying questions, if I can. How many people in your group decided to finally surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know the numbers, but it was a very large column. It was about 200 metres long, and it went two by two in most cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first came to the area where you were able to see Serb soldiers, can you give us any kind of an estimate of how many Serb soldiers you were able to see when you turned yourself in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: According to an estimate, there were at least 50 Serb soldiers. There was a personnel carrier that was parked there, and there were some artillery weapons too, but we didn't dare look at them because we didn't have time. We were running to the place where we had to sit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the first group of Serb soldiers was about 50. Do you know what kind of outfits they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, as worn by the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this group tried to take your money. What about personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about personal belongings that people had with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They seized our personal belongings as well, and if anyone had a hat on his head, they took that off too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly where this area was that you were finally placed, among of rows of people, near the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: This was between Sandici and Kravica, according to my judgement, because I was coming from the other side. But I think it was somewhere between Sandici and Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened once you got there and were put among those rows of other Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we got there, we had to form rows, and then there was a change of shift and they told us some other troops had arrived also wearing camouflage uniforms. Then they said, "These are Arkan's men." I didn't notice any badges on them or not with the words "Arkanovci" on it because we didn't dare look. There were two soldiers to each row. Then one of those soldiers who was on the personnel carrier said, "Don't let me kill you all, and then I could go to The Hague." He knew what "The Hague" meant even then. He was a young man of 25, not more. Then when those soldiers came, they said that they were Arkanovci. They forced us to lie down on our stomachs and then shout, "Long live the King," and we did. Then again they told us to sit up. When we sat up normally, then it was about an hour or an hour and a half before nightfall. I didn't have a watch. Then the gentleman, General Mladic, arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but the interpreters have to interpret everything you're saying in English and French and you're going a little quickly. So if you could try and slow down and give some breaks so I might be able to ask some questions in between.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this second group of soldiers that arrived, the second shift as you've called it --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how many was in that second shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know the number, but I think, again, there were at least 50, because there were two soldiers to each row and there were more than 20 rows, maybe 25. That's why my estimate was about 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, with automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the time that you said Mladic arrived, do you have an estimate of how many Muslim men were sitting in this area where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: At least 2.000, maybe as many as 2.500.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did Mladic arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I didn't have a watch, but it was an hour and a half prior to nightfall, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that time in Bosnia would be roughly what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It would be about 7.30 because it was summertime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to recognise Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I hadn't known Mladic from before, but people who watched television knew him, and I recognised Mladic when I reached free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when Mladic got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When Mladic came, he said, "Good evening, neighbours." We replied, "Good evening." And then he said, "The governments are negotiating, and tomorrow you will all be exchanged for all." We will go to hangars. We won't have any supper, but we will have water ^.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just ask you to slow down a little bit if you could. Anything else that you remember him saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: He said that we would be exchanged the next day, all for all, and he said that we would be given water, that we would go to some hangars. But he didn't say that we would be given any supper, though the previous -- his predecessor said we would be given supper. We thanked him and we applauded him when he promised that he would exchange us the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us how long you -- between the time that Mladic had spoke to you and the time that you first arrived at the meadow, how long had that been? What period of time did you spend on that meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Five or ten minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you at that meadow for the whole day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We were there for about three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any of the Muslim men being abused in any way during those three or four hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No. No one was abused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone transported, any of the Muslim men transported away in any direction by any vehicles or marched away by foot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, they let a woman go and a child, and two young girls, and they let go eight to ten boys between 12 and 14. These were released by one of the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any announcement about young men or how did you know that they picked out boys 12 to 14?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They didn't make any announcements, but the boys of that age would get up. A rather large boy that got up, they told him to sit down because he was big enough to carry a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what happened to those young boys that they picked out of the crowd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Those children were immediately sent by vehicle and they were released. The vehicle went to free territory to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know they were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Because I came across that boy and I asked him and he said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after all this, you ran across one of the boys you saw released in the field in the free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, I hadn't seen him, but I spoke to people I had known, and I met him while I was living in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened after Mladic's little speech was over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When Mladic finished, he left after some 10 or 15 minutes. The vehicles that had taken the women and children to free territory returned. Then we were ordered for the first row to get up and to board the vehicle. Then the first row got up, then the second row, and row by row, I don't remember which row I was in, my turn came. I boarded a trailer of a truck. Then I saw a Serb soldier with a cockade entering and saying that he would board the truck with the driver. He didn't mistreat us, he didn't sit with us. And they drove us --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said you saw a Serb soldier with a something, I didn't quite understand what it was that you saw this Serb soldier have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Cockade, it's a Chetnik badge on a hat that used to be worn by Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this person have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I cannot recollect whether he had a weapon inside the vehicle or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the vehicle that you got into, can you describe what kind of vehicle that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was a truck with a trailer, and I was in the trailer. You know what a truck is and a trailer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what normally is carried in the trailer that you and other men were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: One usually transports coal because the sides were rather high, the kind used for coal or agricultural produce that is light so to avoid it spilling over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the size of this trailer and the height of the sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The trailer was at least 10 metres long and the sides may have been 1.20 metres, 1.40 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how wide was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Probably two and a half to three metres, I don't know exactly. But that would be my estimate that is how wide it should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know roughly how many men were put in the back of this trailer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know. Between 25 and 30 at least could fit, but I don't remember. I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the men standing or sitting or a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They were sitting. All of them were sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while you were sitting in there, the height of the sides of the trailer must have been well over your heads so it would be difficult to see out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell before you actually sat in the trailer how many other vehicles were on either side of the trailer you got into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know. There were some vehicles, but how many, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any way to give us any kind of an estimate? More than three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: More, of course. There may have been 10 or 15 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of vehicles were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: There were trucks, trailers, buses, trucks with trailers, because they were driving women and children in all kinds of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day while you were in that meadow lined up with the men, did you see vehicles go by you on the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We only saw those vehicles taking the women and children. There were no other vehicles on the road at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what direction were the women and children being taken into in vehicles when you were sitting on the meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They were driving them in the direction of Kladanj towards the free territory of the Tuzla region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were put in the back of this trailer, how long were you in the back of the trailer until the truck moved off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It moved off soon after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which direction did it go in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: In the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did it go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We were taken to Bratunac and once we got there, they took us to a man who was a driver, and he said that the buses belonged to the Vihor Transport Company and that the garages that were there were also part of the Vihor Company. But I didn't know the man, I just realised he was a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the man that was in the back of the trailer with you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: He was in the back of the trailer with me, he was in the same trailer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got into the town of Bratunac, how did you know you were in the town if you were down low in the bed of this trailer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, we could see on our left-hand side, because the buildings were three to four floors high. And on the right side, there seemed to have been no buildings at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know roughly what time of day or evening it was when you arrived in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was in the evening at about half past nine. It was already dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you were sitting in the back of this trailer, could you tell how many other vehicles were around your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The vehicles were parked, one after the other. According to my estimate, I know that there were many of them both ahead and behind, and I know that Serb soldiers were looking for men who were on those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know Serb soldiers were looking for the men on the buses both in front of you and behind you? Could you hear it or could you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We could hear them. We could hear them ask about the vehicle, because we didn't know that, we just realised that when they came to our vehicle. First they asked about a village of Pusmulici, near Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who were they asking about this village? Were these people in your vehicle or one of the other vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: In one of the other vehicles that were near us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just able to hear this from where you were sitting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could hear them. They were talking in loud voices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you stand up and look out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, I didn't dare do it. There were Serb soldiers standing guard around the vehicles. Somebody, I remembered, stuck up his hand and was hit on his hand by a rifle butt by someone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the sound of the people outside the vehicles, could you get a rough idea of the number of Serb soldiers outside the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, we couldn't tell the number of those soldiers. We couldn't see them. One of them peeped across the side of the trailer and we could see him. But we couldn't tell how many of them there were around the trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you were telling us earlier. You heard Serb soldiers asking at one of your neighbouring trucks if there was anyone from a particular village. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, they said, "If so and so appears," they would ask for the man's name, surname, and father's name, and then they would take the man to a garage, on which the door was open. At that moment we would hear thuds and people screaming. The man would start to scream, to cry, and then they would shout at him, they would yell at him, and then we could hear fire from an automatic weapon, and then everything would go quiet. This went on throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I know this is very difficult to estimate, but can you give us any idea of how many different Muslim men you heard that were put in a situation where they were taken out to this area nearby you and where you could hear these sounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We were some 30 metres away from the garage and we were able to observe more during the night. But I couldn't tell you the number because they kept taking people away all night. They also hit people near the trucks with their rifle butts, so we could see that as they were taking them, going past our truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to see more during the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, it was because, for example, those who were in the middle could raise, a bit, their heads, they could observe things, but those who were next to the sides of the trailer couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to raise your head at all and look out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. I just had a quick look. I would stick out my head like this [indicates] because the area in the front was a little elevated, and that's how I was able to see what was happening. But I didn't dare to stand up completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any soldiers come to your truck that evening, that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions. First, when a soldier came, he asked for a man and a man replied. He was from the municipality of Srebrenica; he was not from the village they were asking about, so they told him to sit down. Then two other men were taken off our trailer, most probably because they had been recognised. One of them was between 30 and 35 years of age; the other one was a bit younger. Most probably he was immediately recognised, because they asked him about his name -- I don't know whether his name was Omer or whether it was his father's name -- but he was taken on the following morning, and we haven't heard anything about what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother wasn't in the back of the vehicle with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, he wasn't there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you lose track of your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: At the spot where we had gathered while we were sitting on the meadow, and I haven't heard of him ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the men that were in the back of the trailer with you, that spent the night in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I knew only one of them by name. He was also from the Srebrenica municipality. There was nobody from my area, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, I know his name. He was Mehmed, Mehmed Began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the morning came, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When it dawned, we heard them yelling and shouting, saying, "Now you take them to Alija and exchange them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: At that point the trucks started to move, and they were stopped in the outskirts of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to take you briefly back to the meadow. Did they give you any food while you were in that meadow on July 13th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, they didn't give us any food. They only brought water, but it was our people who actually went to get water. But we were not given any food at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were put in the back of this coal truck, were you given any water back there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, the driver who was driving us gave us something, and also a young boy from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been given any food before they gave you water in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the date you surrendered on the meadow July 13th, or do you know the dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The 12th. I think -- the 11th, the 12th. Yes, it was on the 13th, that was the date. It was a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were stopped outside Bratunac? They brought you some water. What else happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They told us that they were waiting for UNPROFOR. So we waited for at least two hours there, on that spot, and a group of Serbian elderly men passed by. Some of them were wearing uniforms; some didn't. They saw some people and they said, "Well, these guys are ours." They probably wanted to take it out on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to see these elderly men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, they were standing on a truck, which was an open kind of truck. It was a FAP truck. It used to be a Yugoslav-produced car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What finally happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, finally after that, after we had been there for about two hours, the column continued in the direction of Konjevic Polje, Drinjaca, and Zvornik, and further on in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your vehicle turn off as it was driving on the road towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we got to Zvornik -- let me stop a little. After we had left Divic, after we had come out of a tunnel, we were told that an UNPROFOR personnel carrier had joined us. It was near the village of Divic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Divic is just south of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in the outskirts of Zvornik, maybe some 800 metres away from the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The soldiers who saw it. At that moment I didn't see the APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers in the back of the vehicle with you at any time during this trek from the meadow up, now, to Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, there were no soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where were these soldiers that actually talked to you and told you about the APC?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Not the soldiers but people who were with us. People talked amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So somebody saw an APC and you were talking amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went on the road towards Tuzla, can you tell us where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we went towards Tuzla, we drove for a short while, and then at one point the truck turned right. I was a little bit familiar with the area, I knew it somewhat better, and I realised that it was moving in the direction of the village of Grbovci. The vehicles were travelling at a very slow place. One by one they reached a schoolyard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to getting to the schoolyard, did you ever take a look out of the back of this truck to tell how many vehicles were travelling along with you, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. When we left Bratunac, we reached a location which is called Avdagina Njive. We climbed a hill, and then when we were on top of the hill, we could actually see how long the column of the vehicles was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to make out how many vehicles were there or how long the column was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The column was a longish one, but I cannot tell you exactly how many vehicles there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough estimate or a rough estimate of how many --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you how long it was, but there were at least 30 vehicles, large vehicles. At least 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: There were trucks, trailer trucks, buses. Most of them were really large vehicles. The idea was to transport as many people as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're at the school. It may be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is really a convenient time. We will have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume with our hearing. Mr. McCloskey, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness L, your vehicle had just arrived at a schoolyard in a place you were familiar with, you called it Grbovci. What happened when your vehicle came to a stop at the schoolyard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we reached the schoolyard, I noticed the UN APC. The letter that was written on it was either "C" or "S". It was something else instead of UNPROFOR. There was only one sign on the APC and there were two soldiers wearing UNPROFOR uniforms. There was also a civilian of 50 to 55 years of age who was walking around with them like an interpreter. These soldiers didn't address us. They were carrying automatic rifles in their hands. So we entered the compound, the yard, and some 30 Serb soldiers were standing there and they ordered us off the trucks. They told us to raise our hands up and to run towards the entrance of the school. When we were outside the entrance, I was ordered by one of their soldiers to take off my leather jacket. There was a large pile of clothes there. So when I got to the hall, I realised that more than half of the people had already been there. Some elderly people were also there who had been brought from Potocari. There were people as old as 70 years of age, maybe more. At that point, we were ordered to sit down. We were crowded; we were pressed against each other. After everybody had got in, we realised that there were four boys there and they were separated and taken to a corner of the hall. The Serb soldiers who were there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you a second.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about what time your vehicle reached the schoolyard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was in the early hours of the afternoon. I didn't have a watch, but it could have been around 1.00, in view of the time when we left Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers that were outside the school, you said there were about 30 of them, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing camouflage uniforms as well. There may have been Serb policemen amongst them here and there, because Serb policemen had grey camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said when you -- what part of the building did you go into when you got into the school building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I sat down in the part of the building which was to the left side of one of the entrances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of room was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was a gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say when you arrived it was half full. Could you give us a rough estimate of how many people "half full" was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Well, it was full. At least 700 or 800 people must have been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first got into the gym, did you see any Serb soldiers inside of the gym? No?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, they were not there. They were only standing at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness -- we have four exhibits, 19/3, 19/2, 19/5, and 19/8. If we could show him those four exhibits in that order, 19/3 first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've had a chance to look at some photographs of a school before coming to testify today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could start with 19/3 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could take a look at this picture. It's a wintertime picture so it's a little different. But do you recognise the building that's depicted in that picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the pointer, can you point out, if you see it, the area where you entered the building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I think it was roughly here [indicates]. This is the gym [indicates], and this is an additional adjacent building, and this is where we entered. We got to this smaller building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, when he pointed to the gym, it was the large building in the back. And there is a smaller building in front that he also made reference to and he said they entered in the area where there appears to be a circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could now look at 19/2. Do you recognise this photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is also the gym. This is the small building with the door in it [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the area where you exited from the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It's here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Indicating the circle on the photo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you now look at 19/5. Do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the inside of the gym [indicates]. This is one of the walls with windows on it [indicates], and pillars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, in particular, about this photo do you recognise from your experience that day in the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I recognise the place by these windows and by the way the inside of the gym looks, because the picture was taken inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could hold off on that last photo for a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived inside the gymnasium, where did you go? Actually, let me stop there and ask you a question before that. I'm sorry. You said that prior to going inside the gymnasium, they made you take off your coat and put it in a pile of clothes. Did you see the soldiers requiring anybody else to take off coats or clothes and put it in this pile?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I didn't see it. I didn't have time to wait.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big of a pile of clothes was it where you put your jacket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was quite big, maybe enough for a passenger vehicle trailer roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got inside the gymnasium, where did they put you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I sat left to the entrance, near the opening where they took us out of the hall later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were put in this gym with all these other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we all entered the hall and no one else was coming in, we sat there for about two or three hours, perhaps, and then some soldiers came and we were ordered to keep silent. So we stopped talking. Then one of those men at the door, I don't know who it was, he ordered four rows at the end of the hall to get up. These were mostly elderly men. Then they ordered them to turn around to the right and face the wall. This went on roughly until they reached my part, and they told us to turn our backs to the exit and to face the wall next to us. Then one of the soldiers said, "These people must not be killed." Then this other Serb soldier said, "And who says so?" And then this soldier --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me interrupt you one second. Who said "These people must not be killed"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: One of us prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then what happened after he said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Then the Serb soldier said, "And who said so?" Then this man repeated what he said. He said, "We'll see," and he told him to get out. The man went out. We heard a shot. The man started screaming. Another shot was heard, and the man fell quiet. Then they took out another man from the other end of the gym. Again, we heard shots and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they took out the second man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to the time that you were first put inside the gymnasium with the other people. Your truckload of men, were they put in the gym with you, the people that you arrived to the school with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did people continue to arrive inside the gymnasium after your group was put in the group or was your group the last group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Our group wasn't the last group. There were others coming in, but when they had all come in, then this, what I just told you, happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after you first arrived did Muslim men continue to be brought into the school, into the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: This may have lasted five or ten or fifteen minutes. The vehicles came one after another. It didn't take hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How full did the gym get when the process of bringing Muslim men in finally finished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It was full. Maybe there would have been two metres that were empty where the four boys were sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of about how many Muslim men were crowded inside this gym that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: According to my estimate, about 2.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you arranged? Were you sitting or standing or lying down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We were sitting, but our knees were touching and so were our shoulders, next to one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this process that they were bringing in more Muslim men into the gym, could you see any Serb soldiers inside the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: They didn't enter the gym; they only stood at the door. And sometimes they would shoot into the wall or the ceiling of the gym.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they would sometimes shoot into the wall or the ceiling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Because it was very warm, people were demanding water. They couldn't bring in a lot of water; they brought us only a little. So people were making noises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any food while you were inside this gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, we didn't. Only water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get enough water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any place to use the toilet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, there was a bucket that was used as a toilet in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about the man that made the comment about don't kill people, and that he was taken out. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: After that they stopped bringing us water. And then the same thing continued, the same situation. The Serb soldiers were at the door. People were addressing them "Soldiers", but they would answer, "We're not soldiers; we are Karadzic's young Chetniks," because they were very young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you make out anything from their uniforms, anything special about them or anything different, the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No. Most of them were bareheaded. They had camouflage uniforms like the other Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: After that, at the opening to the left, there were two Serb soldiers standing there and a Serb woman in uniform. They brought a pile of rags with which they tied our eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, do you recall about what time they first brought this pile of rags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I think it was shortly after these Serb officers, or whatever, had arrived, I don't know, those who had ordered those rearrangements. There were these pieces of cloth; they were about 60 centimetres long, five or six centimetres wide; they were mostly patterned so you couldn't see through them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were there, or how big a pile of rags were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Like a sack full, shall we say, if you were to pour the contents out of a sack on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it look like it would be enough to blindfold everybody in the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Probably. Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 19/8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a look at that photograph and tell us if you recognise anything in there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I recognise it. This is the exit [indicates]; this is the hall [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When he said "This is the exit," he pointed to the doorway where number 2 is marked with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "That's the exit" --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is that where the Serb soldiers were standing, and the woman you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What occurred when these soldiers and the woman soldier were standing by that exit and they brought in all these strips of cloth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Then they assigned one to blindfold the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assigned one. Who? A Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Then what happened was that once we were blindfolded we had to leave this room and form a letter "L". This woman of Serb ethnicity, in a camouflage uniform like any other soldier, would give us each a glass or a cupful of water while we were there blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see people get blindfolded in front of you that left through this exit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell where they were going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: People asked, "Where are you taking these people?" and they said, "We're taking them to the Bijeljina Logor, to Bijeljina, to a camp," but it wasn't a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take until it was your turn to get blindfolded and go out this exit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: At least three hours, if not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were blindfolded and given the water, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: We got into a Tamic brand truck, with signs either of the police or the army. I could see through the blindfold. They were Cyrillic registration plates; they were not civilian registration plates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well were you able to see through the blindfold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: One could see about 50 per cent and more, because they weren't so strict about us moving the blindfold off our eyes for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court what a TAM truck is and what this TAM truck looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It's a small truck, of two and a half tonnes carrying capacity, manufactured in Slovenia, during the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the back of the truck look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It has sides of some 40 to 50 centimetres which can be closed, and there was canvas over it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any place to sit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: There were two benches. When the benches were full, then people sat in between the two benches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this truck parked in relation to where the school exit was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Next to the room where they were blindfolding us. There was a kind of obstacle in front of the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken directly from the room onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell how many other Muslim men were put in the back of this truck with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: There were up to 30, maybe more, because eight to ten men could sit on the benches and the space in between is broader than the benches themselves so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did they put men in the spaces in between the benches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you tell that if you were blindfolded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we were in the truck, we took off the blindfolds because we believed we were going to Bijeljina. We thought they wouldn't mistreat us. And when the engine got started again, we put back our blindfolds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serb soldiers in the back of this truck with you, crowded full of Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the truck went, as far as you could make out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: The truck drove for a very short while. According to my judgement, it took a left turn to a macadam road, because we could tell by the shaking in the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It took a left turn from the macadam road onto a bumpier road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, from the asphalt road onto the macadam road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The macadam road is bumpier than the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you got on the macadam road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we got there the truck stopped, and we immediately heard people talking behind our backs. We noticed some dead people as we were looking down towards the ground. Through the cloth we could see some dead people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what you yourself were able to see, looking down through your blindfold, as you were getting off the truck.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I personally saw a dead man. I'm only talking about myself; I'm not saying what other people saw. I saw this dead man in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Then they lined us up and they started with bursts of fire from my right-hand side, and then men were falling to the left. Men brought me down, so that a man covered this part of my face [indicates], and he fell before me and my arm was over his chest. That was probably the last shot fired in a standing position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody on top of you or near you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Yes, this one who was on top of me, because on my back there was a bloodstain from this man who was on top of me, and the blood was dripping from him onto me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel him die, or did he die instantly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I didn't. But one man, I don't know whether he was in my group or a group after me, he said, "Finish me off," and then this Serb soldier said, "Slowly. Slowly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else happened as you were lying there amongst this carnage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: When we had all fallen to the ground, then one of them came and fired single shots at the people who were probably moving. Then a stone injured me slightly that probably jumped off of the road. It was a small injury and it didn't hurt. If it had been a bullet, it would have been more painful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Then those Serb soldiers were shouting, "Let's take their watches off their hands so we can get beer instead," but another one said, "Don't," and they didn't. And I didn't have a watch anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: Then another truck came, and again you only heard shots, and people were probably falling but there weren't many cries or screams. So we come to almost nightfall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see the arrival of other trucks or were you still blindfolded at this point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: No, I still had the blindfold, and I was lying on my stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you look up at all at this point, when the other trucks started arriving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't dare because I didn't know what was behind my back. I didn't dare move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long this process, where trucks arrived and you could hear gunfire, how long that kept going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L
utterances.text: It went on late into the night, but the exact hour I'm not able to tell. But it went on into the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the story, of course, goes on a little further. Do you wish to continue the story tomorrow or try to go further today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do you need, roughly, Mr. McCloskey, to finish with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes, maybe thirty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, we will finish for today and we'll resume tomorrow at 9.30. I think the parties already have a proposed timetable for our Status Conference for Thursday. Therefore, I'd like you to look at that proposal closely. I'm telling the Defence that we have considered your motion. We're going to have a month and a half now, and then after that we will have more time. And I think that will correspond to the amount of time you have requested. But in any case we will reconsider that at the Status Conference on Thursday, and all I'm asking is that you look at that proposal closely. Therefore, Witness, you are going to stay tomorrow, when we will resume. So we will resume the hearing tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.34 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of April, 2000, the 9.30 a.m.
